title: Canada's $500 Billion Defence Spending Surge Just Opened the Door to India. Here's What's Actually on the Table.
excerpt: High Commissioner Christopher Cooter describes a 'hockey stick' trajectory in military spending and a 'transformative' partnership after years of diplomatic freeze
body:
Canada's defence spending is about to follow what its top diplomat in New Delhi calls a "hockey stick" trajectory. India is invited to ride the curve.

In an interview with ANI, Canadian High Commissioner to India Christopher Cooter laid out a vision of a "transformative" defence and industrial partnership between Ottawa and New Delhi — one anchored by a historic surge in Canadian military expenditure that he says will create unprecedented opportunities for Indian aerospace and defence firms.

"Actually, it's a very small relationship," Cooter said of the current bilateral defence trade. "The defence industry in Canada is quite large. But I can tell you that we are on a trajectory that looks like a Canadian hockey stick."

$500 Billion and Counting

Canada recently crossed the NATO-standard two-percent-of-GDP defence spending threshold and is now fast-tracking toward five percent. For the world's ninth-largest economy, that commitment translates to roughly $500 billion in additional military spending by 2035 — a figure that dwarfs anything Ottawa has invested in defence in decades.

"We have lots of advanced technology, but we don't have the scale, we don't have the market," Cooter explained. India, with the world's second-largest armed forces and a defence manufacturing ecosystem that has pushed exports past $4 billion annually, has precisely what Canada lacks.

The proposition is straightforward: Canadian technological innovation married to Indian industrial manufacturing capacity.

> ""We have lots of advanced technology, but we don't have the scale, we don't have the market," Cooter explained."

From Freeze to Forward Motion

The overture would have been unthinkable 18 months ago. Under former Prime Minister Justin Trudeau, India-Canada relations hit their lowest point in decades over the Khalistan dispute, culminating in the mutual expulsion of diplomats in late 2023. Canadian High Commissioner and Indian High Commissioner posts were both left vacant.

The reset began with Mark Carney's election as Prime Minister. Carney visited India in February 2026, meeting Modi at Hyderabad House, where the two leaders announced a formal India-Canada Defence Dialogue — the first institutional framework for bilateral military cooperation in the countries' history. Defence attachés have since been appointed on both sides.

![New Delhi — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fe/Forecourt%2C_Rashtrapati_Bhavan_-_1.jpg/3840px-Forecourt%2C_Rashtrapati_Bhavan_-_1.jpg)

Cooter, who took up his post in August 2025 as the first High Commissioner after the diplomatic freeze, described the relationship as having entered a "reliable, process-driven phase."

What's Actually on the Table

The emerging partnership extends across several domains:

The General Security of Information Agreement (GSOIA), currently being negotiated, would create a government-backed framework for handling sensitive defence information — a prerequisite for joint ventures in classified technologies.

Maritime security cooperation, including bilateral and multilateral naval exercises, has been flagged as a priority area, reflecting shared interests in Indo-Pacific stability.

Beyond hardware, Cooter highlighted collaboration on combating fentanyl precursor supply chains — a major domestic issue in Canada that traces back to chemical suppliers in Asia — and dismantling international scam call centres that target citizens in both countries.

"We've progressed now in that security dialogue to manage the bilateral irritants more effectively, but also to look beyond to see where we can cooperate on a regional or a global basis," Cooter said.

Why the Diaspora Should Care

For the 1.8 million Canadians of Indian origin — the largest visible minority group in Canada — the rapprochement carries both symbolic and material significance. The diplomatic freeze had chilled people-to-people exchanges, complicated visa processing, and cast a shadow over the community's dual identity.

Stronger institutional ties translate to more stable visa regimes, more predictable trade corridors for Indian professionals in Canada's growing defence sector, and a diplomatic relationship that is less vulnerable to being hijacked by a single issue. The upcoming Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA), expected to conclude in 2026, will further cement the economic dimension.

With India's defence exports having surged from $80 million in 2014 to over $4 billion last year, and BrahMos missile deals signed with Vietnam and Indonesia in the wake of the India-Pakistan conflict, the opportunity Cooter is describing is not hypothetical. The question is whether the political will that produced the thaw can sustain a genuine industrial partnership — or whether the next bilateral irritant sends relations back to the deep freeze.
